knowledge_checks.title: Active Recall: 3.2.7
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. Which statement correctly describes a confidence interval for a mean difference from paired data?
hints: Use the concept from this learning objective only.
knowledge_checks.explanation: Paired analysis works on differences within pairs. Independent two-sample formulas ignore the dependence that pairing creates. Bootstrap CI construction is a different method.
knowledge_checks.model_answer: Analyse paired differences with a one-sample CI for the mean difference.
knowledge_checks.common_mistake: Running an independent two-sample CI on paired columns.

choices.label: Form within-pair differences and construct a one-sample CI for the mean of those differences. Pairing exploits dependence between matched observations and is not the same as an independent two-sample analysis.
Apply the independent two-sample mean-difference CI to the before column and the after column, because pairing only affects the labels.
Ignore the pairing and average all before values against all after values with a pooled variance that assumes independence.
Paired mean-difference CIs are identical to bootstrap confidence intervals; resampling replaces forming differences.

knowledge_checks.title: Checkpoint: 3.2.7
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. Each policyholder has a before/after loss pair (Xᵢ, Yᵢ). Which statement is correct?
knowledge_checks.body: Paired differences; refuse independent two-sample on paired rows.
hints: Use the concept from this learning objective only.
knowledge_checks.explanation: Matched pairs → differences → one-sample CI for the mean difference. Equal column lengths do not justify an independent two-sample analysis of paired rows.
knowledge_checks.model_answer: Analyse Dᵢ = Yᵢ − Xᵢ with a one-sample CI for μ_D; refuse independent two-sample on paired columns.
knowledge_checks.common_mistake: Using the independent two-sample interval on paired before/after columns.

choices.label: Form Dᵢ = Yᵢ − Xᵢ (or Xᵢ − Yᵢ) and build a one-sample CI for μ_D. Applying the independent two-sample formula to the before and after columns ignores pairing and uses the wrong variance structure.
Compute x̄ and ȳ separately and use a two-sample CI for μ_Y − μ_X that assumes independent samples, because each column has the same length.
The paired CI is formed for μ_X and μ_Y separately; no difference parameter is involved.
Pairing means you must discard half the data at random so that the remaining before and after values are independent.

worked_example.title: Paired t-interval for before/after loss reduction
worked_example.problem_statement: Eight policyholders each have a before/after loss pair. Differences d = before − after (£00) are: 12, 8, −2, 15, 10, 5, 9, 7. Using t_{7, 0.975} = 2.365, construct a 95% CI for the mean difference μ_d.
worked_example.attempt_before_reveal: CMP closed. Reduce to a one-sample t-interval on the differences.

steps.label: Mean difference
steps.explanation: Paired data are analysed through the differences d_i.

steps.label: Sample SD of differences
steps.explanation: The SE uses the sample SD of the paired differences, not the raw before/after series.

steps.label: SE and interval
steps.attempt_cue: SE = s_d/√n; then d̄ ± t × SE.
steps.explanation: One-sample t formula applied to the differences.

worked_example.common_pitfall: Treating the before and after samples as independent two-sample data instead of pairing, or using z = 1.96 with n = 8.
